analysis.one_liner: Requires federal facilities to follow the same hazardous waste laws as private companies, with EPA inspections, fines, and public records.
analysis.headline: Backed by 52 cosponsors, the Senate passed the bill's substance 94-3 on October 24, 1991 by folding it into a companion House bill, then indefinitely postponed S. 596 itself; the record shown includes no House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal facilities — military bases, nuclear weapons plants, and other government sites — had been largely exempt from the hazardous waste laws that private companies must obey. This bill required every federal agency to assess hazardous releases at its waste sites, subjected them to annual EPA inspections with public groundwater monitoring records, waived the government's sovereign immunity so it could be fined and ordered to clean up like any private party, and allowed EPA to bring enforcement actions even against the legislative and judicial branches.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near the hundreds of hazardous waste sites run by federal agencies — military bases, Energy Department nuclear plants, and other government installations — where contaminated groundwater was a documented risk. States and the EPA gain the power to inspect, fine, and order cleanups at these sites, and inspection records become public.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near federal hazardous waste sites

how_it_helps.text: Requires each federal agency to assess hazardous substance releases from its waste management units, state whether the facility complies with the major environmental laws, and file the assessments with the EPA and the state where the facility sits.
Directs the EPA Administrator to inspect every covered federal facility annually, including an analysis of groundwater monitoring, and to make the inspection records available to the public.
Waives the federal government's sovereign immunity under the Solid Waste Disposal Act, so agencies can face administrative orders, civil penalties, and fines the same as a private polluter.

Authorizes the EPA Administrator to start enforcement actions against any federal department or agency — including the executive, legislative, and judicial branches — in the same manner as against any other person.

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies — and ultimately taxpayers — who must reimburse EPA for inspection costs, pay civil penalties and fines, and fund cleanups. Federal employees can now be personally charged under federal and state solid and hazardous waste laws, though agencies may represent or reimburse them for acts within the scope of their jobs.

drawbacks.text: Makes federal employees personally subject to criminal sanctions, including fines and imprisonment, under federal or state solid and hazardous waste laws for acts within their official duties.

Limits a surety company's liability on bonds for federal hazardous-substance cleanup contracts to the cost of completing the work, so if a contractor defaults, the government absorbs more of the loss.

Lets the EPA Administrator grant variances from mixed-waste (hazardous plus radioactive) treatment rules where treatment technology or capacity is not available, which could delay compliance at nuclear waste sites beyond 1993.
Because federal agencies pay inspection reimbursements, fines, and cleanups out of public budgets, the bill's costs on polluting agencies are ultimately borne by taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: the government must follow the same waste laws it imposes on private companies, and communities next to federal sites get annual inspections, groundwater monitoring, and public records. The costs are real but bounded — fines and cleanups come from public budgets and employees face personal criminal exposure, softened by agency-paid representation. The Senate version also quietly narrows the bill's bite in two places: it caps surety companies' liability on federal cleanup-contract bonds and allows variances where mixed nuclear waste cannot yet be treated.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the substance of the bill 94-3 by incorporating it as an amendment into a companion House bill and passing that instead, then indefinitely postponed S. 596 itself; the provided record ends there, with no House vote shown.

narrative.text: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee reported the bill without amendment on May 30, 1991, and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
The bill sat on the calendar through the summer; when the Senate finally moved to it in October 1991, a cloture motion — a vote to cut off debate — was needed just to proceed to consideration.
On October 17, 1991, the Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed 85-14: all 57 Democrats present voted yes, while 14 of 43 Republicans voted no.
On October 24, 1991, the Senate passed companion bill H.R. 2194 in lieu of S. 596, 94-3, incorporating this measure as an amendment, and then indefinitely postponed S. 596 itself.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities and states pressing to hold federal polluters to the same rules came out ahead in the near term, since the substance cleared the Senate 94-3. Federal agencies gained time with no House vote shown in the record, and surety companies gained a new liability limit added in the Senate version.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near federal waste sites, so far

sides.party_line_note: The bill was broadly bipartisan — 52 cosponsors including 8 Republicans and a 94-3 passage vote — but every no vote on record came from Republicans (14 of 43 against the cloture motion, 3 of 43 against passage), while no Democrat voted no on either vote.

industries.industry: Federal agencies as hazardous waste site operators (Defense, Energy, and others)
industries.note: The bill ends their exemption from solid and hazardous waste law: they face annual EPA inspections, fines, administrative orders, and cleanup duties at sites ranging from military bases to nuclear weapons plants. Their compliance costs come out of public budgets, but the communities living next to those sites get the protection.

The Senate version caps a surety's liability on bonds for federal hazardous-substance cleanup contracts at the cost of completing the work, so if a contractor defaults, the government and taxpayers absorb more of the loss. It applies only to bonds executed between October 1991 and December 1992 and excludes sites on the Superfund priority list.

industries.industry: Energy services firms and electric and natural gas utilities
industries.note: Title IV directs the Architect of the Capitol to retrofit the Capitol and congressional office buildings and encourages energy-saving performance contracts with private firms plus demand-management and conservation programs negotiated with electric and gas utilities — paid work for those companies that also cuts federal energy use.

The bill requires EPA to set treatment standards for mixed hazardous-radioactive waste and pushes federal facilities toward actual treatment by 1993, creating demand for treatment technologies and capacity.
